cards.title: RBI's rate-setting committee begins its 3-day meeting today, with markets betting on a hold at 5.25%
cards.what_happened: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee began its three-day rate-setting meeting today, August 3, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra due to announce the decision on August 5. A Reuters survey of 72 economists found overwhelming consensus for a hold: 68 expect the repo rate to remain unchanged at **5.25%**, four expect a 25-basis-point hike, and none expect a cut. The committee is weighing elevated crude oil prices — worsened by the ongoing Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions — and monsoon-driven food-price risk against recent strong growth data, with SBI Research raising its Q1 growth estimate to roughly 7% just a day before the meeting began.
key_points: The RBI's **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** meets August 3–5; Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** announces the decision on August 5.
A Reuters poll of 72 economists found **68 expect the repo rate to stay at 5.25%**, only 4 expect a hike, none expect a cut.
The repo rate was last cut by **25 basis points to 5.25%** in December 2025.
The committee is balancing **rising inflation risk** from Gulf oil prices and an uneven monsoon against **strong growth** — SBI Research just raised its Q1 growth estimate to around 7%.
Expect the RBI to keep its policy stance **'neutral'** but strike a more hawkish tone in its commentary.
cards.moot: Central banks don't just react to inflation and growth numbers — they react to risk, so an oil-price shock happening on the other side of the world can shape an interest-rate decision that affects loan payments in India, even before it shows up in official inflation data.

depth.background: India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, sets the country's benchmark interest rate — the **repo rate**, the rate at which it lends to commercial banks — through a six-member Monetary Policy Committee that meets roughly every two months. The RBI's job is to balance keeping inflation in check with supporting economic growth; it cut rates in December 2025 to help growth, and has held steady since. This meeting lands at an unusually complicated moment: the Strait of Hormuz crisis (see our linked story) has kept crude oil prices elevated for months, directly feeding into India's import bill and inflation, while heavy monsoon flooding in Assam, Kerala, and Gujarat adds further uncertainty to food prices and growth.
depth.why_it_matters: The repo rate influences borrowing costs across the Indian economy — from home loans and business credit to how much the government pays to borrow — so the RBI's decision affects millions of Indians with loans or savings tied to bank interest rates. A hawkish tone alongside a hold would signal the RBI sees inflation risk as serious enough to keep future rate cuts off the table for now.
depth.ripple_effects: If the RBI holds as expected but flags inflation risk from oil prices, banks are likely to keep loan and deposit rates roughly steady in the near term, and equity markets may react more to the tone of the accompanying statement than to the decision itself. A resolution of the Strait of Hormuz crisis (see our linked global story) would ease the oil-price pressure that is the biggest swing factor in this decision.
depth.why_now: The MPC meets on a fixed roughly-bi-monthly schedule, and this cycle happens to fall right as global oil-price risk from the Hormuz crisis and domestic monsoon flooding are both peaking, making this a more closely watched meeting than usual.
depth.watch_next: Watch for Governor Malhotra's policy statement on August 5, especially any change in language around inflation risk and the outlook for future rate moves.
depth.market_link: A hold at 5.25% is largely priced in; a hawkish tone could weigh on rate-sensitive sectors like banking, real estate, and autos, while a surprise hike would be more clearly negative for equities and bond prices.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks — the RBI's main tool for controlling how expensive or cheap borrowing is across the economy.
The six-member RBI committee that meets periodically to set India's benchmark interest rate.

cards.title: Assam's flood death toll climbs to 82 as Kerala reports 8 deaths in a separate monsoon crisis
cards.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll rose to **82** as monsoon rains and river swelling continued to batter the northeastern state, with more than **6,53,100 people affected across 11 districts**, according to state disaster authorities. Separately, and unrelated geographically, Kerala reported at least **8 deaths** from days of relentless rain, landslides and flash floods, concentrated in the state's high ranges — four of the deaths came from landslides in **Kottayam and Idukki districts** alone. Search operations are ongoing for **6 missing fishermen** (four from Thiruvananthapuram, two from Kollam) swept out into the Arabian Sea, plus two Kannur residents swept away by a river. Kerala has moved over **5,700 people** into relief camps, and the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an **orange alert for 12 districts** warning of continued intense rainfall.
key_points: Assam's flood toll has risen from 80 to **82 dead**, with over **6.53 lakh people affected** across 11 districts.
Kerala separately reports **8 dead** from landslides and flash floods, with **8 more missing**.
Six missing Kerala fishermen were swept out to sea near Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam.
The IMD has issued fresh **rain warnings** for Assam, Kerala, Gujarat and Chhattisgarh as the monsoon intensifies nationwide.
The Centre has pre-deployed **NDRF teams** and is coordinating relief with state governments.
cards.moot: Disaster response in a country as large as India often means managing multiple, unrelated crises simultaneously — capacity built for one flood-prone region can't simply be redirected to another hit at the same time.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Assam's flood toll at 80 dead, with the government announcing a six-month loan moratorium for affected families.
thread.changed: The toll has since risen to 82, and a second, separate flood emergency has emerged in Kerala with 8 dead and 8 missing, including 6 fishermen swept out to sea.

depth.background: India's June-September monsoon is a lifeline for its farm economy but also its biggest recurring disaster risk, with the northeast (Assam) and the southwest coast (Kerala) both especially flood- and landslide-prone due to heavy terrain rainfall. Assam's flood toll had already reached **80** as of yesterday, prompting the government to announce a six-month loan moratorium for affected families. The crisis has since widened rather than eased, now stretching across multiple, unrelated states simultaneously.
depth.why_it_matters: Two separate, simultaneous flood emergencies on opposite sides of the country show how widespread this year's monsoon disruption has become, straining state disaster-response capacity and national relief resources at the same time.
depth.ripple_effects: Prolonged flooding damages crops, roads and homes, often triggering local food-price spikes and displacement that can last weeks after the water recedes; repeated disaster declarations also pressure state and central budgets already committed to loan moratoriums and relief spending.
depth.why_now: Both crises reflect an unusually intense monsoon spell hitting multiple regions of India at once, with the IMD warning the wider pattern of heavy rain is continuing rather than tapering off.
depth.watch_next: Watch the search for the six missing Kerala fishermen and whether Assam's toll climbs further as flood waters recede and more casualties are confirmed.

cards.title: Lewis Hamilton welcomes new puppy Halo during F1's summer break

It's his first dog since the loss of his beloved English bulldog **Roscoe**, who died of pneumonia last September at 13 years old. To help raise Halo, Hamilton hired **Kirstin McMillian**, a Los Angeles-based, three-generation animal trainer who previously worked with both Roscoe and his other dog, Coco. McMillian reportedly flew to Maine to begin preparing Halo before bringing her back to Los Angeles. The news went viral after Hamilton's partner, Kim Kardashian, posted the first photo of the puppy online, drawing heavy attention during F1's quiet summer break.

It's his first dog since English bulldog **Roscoe** died of pneumonia last September at age **13**

cards.moot: Even in a sport built on speed and technology, personal stories about its stars can dominate headlines when there's no racing to report, showing how much of sports media is about the people, not just the competition.

Hamilton is dating media personality **Kim Kardashian**, and the couple's public life draws attention well beyond racing. cards.title: Audi shelves further F1 engine upgrades until 2027, blaming the budget cap
cards.what_happened: Audi racing director **Allan McNish** said the team will not bring a second power-unit upgrade before the 2026 season ends, having already used its one opportunity at the **Barcelona Grand Prix** in June. That update focused mainly on "driveability" — how smoothly the engine responds to throttle input — rather than outright horsepower, according to driver Nico Hulkenberg. McNish said the bigger, more powerful parts are being held back for **2027** because Audi simply doesn't have the budget to develop this year's and next year's engines at the same time within F1's cost cap. Asked whether the 2027 engine would be a big performance leap, McNish joked "That's '27... we're only halfway through '26," but confirmed it will mostly be new hardware rather than a quick fix. Audi qualified for F1's ADUO catch-up system — which grants extra development chances to manufacturers measured more than 4% off the fastest engine — earning two upgrade windows this year and two more in 2027. Even without more power, Audi's chassis has held up: the team has scored points in three consecutive races, with Gabriel Bortoleto (8 points) and Nico Hulkenberg (2 points) helping it edge past Williams for eighth in the constructors' championship.
key_points: Audi racing director Allan McNish confirmed the team won't bring a **second** power-unit upgrade before 2026 ends
Audi already used its one upgrade at the **Barcelona Grand Prix**, aimed mainly at driveability, not raw power
Bigger engine parts are being saved for **2027** because Audi can't afford to develop both years' engines within F1's roughly **$190 million** cost cap
Audi qualified for F1's catch-up rule (ADUO) after being measured more than **4%** off the pace-setting engine, earning two upgrade windows in 2026 and two more in 2027
Despite the underpowered engine, Audi has scored points in **three straight races**, passing Williams for 8th in the constructors' standings
cards.moot: Even a deep-pocketed manufacturer can't out-develop a strict budget cap — it has to choose between fixing today's problem or building tomorrow's car, a trade-off every team faces in F1's cost-controlled era.

depth.background: Audi entered Formula 1 in 2026 as a full manufacturer, taking over the former Sauber team and building its first power unit from scratch. Team boss is ex-Ferrari chief **Mattia Binotto**, who has always said the engine wouldn't be competitive immediately and that Audi's real goal is fighting for titles by **2030**. Under F1's 2026 rules, most engine development is frozen except for a new mechanism called **ADUO**, which hands lagging manufacturers limited catch-up upgrades. Every manufacturer also has to fit all of this inside a strict shared **cost cap** covering both engine and chassis work.
depth.why_it_matters: It's a rare, candid admission from a brand-new manufacturer that money — not just engineering — dictates when a struggling engine gets fixed, and it confirms Audi's power deficit won't close before 2027 at the earliest. That gives established engine makers more breathing room this season while Audi banks resources for a bigger swing next year.
depth.ripple_effects: With engine gains capped, Audi's points this season will keep depending almost entirely on chassis performance and driver execution from Bortoleto and Hulkenberg. The saved-up 2027 upgrade tokens will combine with F1's next major engine and aero rule reset, potentially reshuffling the competitive order. It's also a signal to sponsors and Audi's board, who've been told to expect a real title fight only by 2030.
depth.why_now: McNish's comments surfaced during F1's summer shutdown, as teams and press review the first half of 2026 and look ahead to preparations for the 2027 regulation reset.
depth.watch_next: Whether Audi's points streak continues without a power boost when racing resumes at the Dutch Grand Prix on August 21.

A yearly spending limit every F1 team and engine maker must stay under, which forces hard choices about what to develop and when.

cards.title: Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon concede Williams won't hit its 2026 targets despite a recovery plan
cards.what_happened: Speaking on Williams' own **Team Torque** podcast, Sainz and Albon gave a sober midseason assessment: the team is making progress behind the scenes, but neither expects a dramatic turnaround once racing resumes at Zandvoort later this month. cards.moot: In sports governed by periodic rule resets, a strong prior season can mask underlying weaknesses that resurface the moment the rules change — real competitiveness is tested across regulation eras, not within one.

depth.background: Williams, one of Formula 1's most storied constructors, had been on a genuine upward curve under team principal James Vowles, capped by a strong 2025 season that raised hopes of a real title challenge. Formula 1 reset its technical rulebook for 2026 — new power units and chassis regulations — which shuffles the competitive order and can undo a team's hard-won progress overnight if its car concept doesn't suit the new rules.
depth.why_it_matters: It's a signal of which teams have genuinely adapted to F1's new rules and which haven't — Williams' 2025 promise made it a team many expected to kick on, and this admission tempers those expectations heading into the second half of the season.
depth.ripple_effects: A prolonged slump could reignite driver-market speculation around Sainz's future and dent sponsor and investor confidence in Williams' rebuild; it also affects the competitive picture other midfield teams are measuring themselves against.

thread.previously: We reported that Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll had identified Williams driver Carlos Sainz as his top target to replace Fernando Alonso, with design chief Adrian Newey personally pushing for the signing, and that Sainz's own decision partly hinged on gains from Williams' upcoming upgrade package.

depth.background: Carlos Sainz joined Williams for the 2025 season after being replaced at Ferrari by Lewis Hamilton, aiming to help rebuild the historic team. cards.title: Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur bans 'championship fight' talk inside the team as the title race hinges on fine margins
cards.what_happened: According to reporting from Italian outlet Gazzetta dello Sport, **Fred Vasseur** has instructed people inside Ferrari not to use the phrase **'world championship fight'** when discussing the team's 2026 season, even as Ferrari remains mathematically in title contention. Vasseur has said publicly that Ferrari's ability to sustain its **current rate of car development** through the second half of the season will determine whether it can mount a serious title challenge, rather than any single big upgrade. He has described the gap to the front of the field as just **'1-2 tenths'** of a second, framing the fight as won or lost in small increments rather than one decisive breakthrough. The comments come as Ferrari enters F1's mid-season **summer break**, a mandatory shutdown period when all teams pause factory work simultaneously.
key_points: Ferrari team principal **Fred Vasseur** has reportedly banned staff from using the words **'world championship fight'** inside the team.
Vasseur says Ferrari's title hopes depend on **sustaining its current development rate** through the rest of the season.
He has said the team is only **'1-2 tenths'** of a second away from the front, a tiny margin in F1 terms.
The approach favors **steady, race-by-race progress** over publicly declaring a title campaign.
This comes as Ferrari enters F1's **summer break**, a mid-season pause when teams regroup and plan upgrades.
cards.moot: Managing internal expectations and messaging can be as important to a team's performance as the technical work itself — how pressure is framed inside an organization shapes how people perform under it.

depth.background: In Formula 1, being only **'1-2 tenths' of a second** off the pace sounds tiny, but at the sport's highest level that gap is the difference between winning and finishing outside the podium — cars are so finely tuned that fractions of a second separate the front of the grid from the middle. **Ferrari**, one of F1's most historic and pressured teams, has a long history of raising fan and media expectations early in a season only to fall short, which can create internal pressure that some team bosses believe hurts performance. **Fred Vasseur** has led Ferrari since 2023 and has generally tried to manage expectations more carefully than some of his predecessors.
depth.why_it_matters: This is a deliberate management choice about how to handle pressure inside a historically pressure-prone team — betting that quiet, steady execution beats public declarations of title intent. For a team with Ferrari's history of technical and strategic errors under pressure, this internal messaging discipline could matter as much as the car's actual pace.
depth.ripple_effects: If Ferrari's low-key approach works and the team stays competitive into the second half of the season, expect more scrutiny on whether Hamilton and his teammate can convert small pace gains into race wins. If it doesn't work, Vasseur's expectation-management strategy itself will likely draw criticism from Italian media, which closely scrutinizes Ferrari's every decision.
depth.why_now: The comments surface as Ferrari heads into the summer break, the natural moment for team bosses to set the tone and expectations for the second half of the season.
depth.watch_next: Watch how Ferrari's pace compares to rivals at the first post-break race in the Netherlands (August 21-23) — that will be the first real test of whether the '1-2 tenths' gap has actually closed.

key_terms.definition: A mandatory multi-week shutdown period in F1 (usually in August) when all teams must stop nearly all factory development work at the same time.

cards.title: Mercedes boss Toto Wolff rules out Verstappen for 2027 — but leaves the door open to pairing him with Antonelli later
cards.what_happened: **Toto Wolff**, Mercedes' team principal, confirmed that **George Russell and Kimi Antonelli** will continue as the team's driver pairing for the **2027 season**, closing the door on any near-term Verstappen move to Mercedes. However, Wolff added that a future **Verstappen-Antonelli partnership** at Mercedes remains a real possibility beyond 2027, saying the team is **'not afraid to make it happen one day.'** The comments come as Antonelli, just **19 years old**, has become this season's breakout star — leading the drivers' championship after multiple wins, including his **sixth win of the season** at the Belgian Grand Prix, ahead of both Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and his own teammate Russell. Verstappen, by contrast, is having an unusually difficult season, sitting **seventh in the standings without a win**, though he remains under contract with Red Bull through **2028** with clauses that could let him leave early depending on performance.
key_points: **Toto Wolff** confirmed **George Russell and Kimi Antonelli** will remain Mercedes' driver lineup for **2027**.
That rules out **Max Verstappen** joining Mercedes next season, despite persistent speculation.
But Wolff said Mercedes would **'not shy away'** from pairing Verstappen and Antonelli together **at some point in the future**.
**Antonelli, 19,** currently **leads the championship**, ahead of Ferrari's Hamilton and teammate Russell.
**Verstappen sits seventh** in the standings, still without a race win this season.
cards.moot: In competitive team sports, a rising young star can reshape a veteran star's leverage almost overnight — Antonelli's success gives Mercedes options it didn't have a year ago, changing the calculus for everyone else in the market.

depth.background: Formula 1's driver market runs on a mix of contracts and speculation — teams often lock in lineups a year or more ahead, and rumors about star drivers switching teams are a constant subplot of every season. **Max Verstappen**, a multiple world champion, has been the subject of persistent rumors about leaving **Red Bull**, the team he's driven for his whole F1 career, partly because his current deal is believed to include performance-linked exit clauses. Meanwhile, **Kimi Antonelli**, a 19-year-old Italian driver in only his second F1 season, has emerged as the surprise story of 2026 — leading the championship at Mercedes, the team that famously dominated F1 in the mid-2010s under Wolff's leadership.
depth.why_it_matters: This confirms Mercedes' lineup stability for next season while keeping alive one of F1's most talked-about hypothetical driver pairings — putting a multiple champion alongside the sport's most exciting rookie talent. It also underlines how far Verstappen's stock has fallen this season relative to Antonelli's rise, a genuine changing-of-the-guard narrative in F1.
depth.ripple_effects: This narrows the list of seats Verstappen could realistically move to for 2027 if he does leave Red Bull, potentially strengthening his negotiating position to stay or pushing him toward a different team. It also raises Antonelli's profile and value heading into contract renewal conversations down the line, since he's now spoken of as a long-term cornerstone alongside a driver of Verstappen's caliber.
depth.why_now: Wolff's comments were made as driver-market speculation heats up during F1's summer break, when teams and drivers use the quiet period to signal their plans for the following season.
depth.watch_next: Watch Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix later this month (Zandvoort, August 21-23), where his own future is expected to become clearer.

key_terms.definition: A condition in a driver's contract that lets them leave a team early if certain performance targets (like finishing position in the championship) aren't met.

cards.title: Hadjar says it's 'a bit sad' that F1's 2026 rules turn classic tracks like Spa into some of the worst on the calendar
cards.what_happened: Red Bull driver **Isack Hadjar** said it is 'a bit sad' that F1's 2026-spec cars have effectively re-ranked the calendar's circuits based on how much energy they let cars recover and redeploy, rather than by the quality of racing itself. He singled out **Spa-Francorchamps**, historically one of the sport's most respected tracks, as now among the worst-suited under the new regulations. By contrast, he praised the recent **Hungarian Grand Prix** as feeling like 'classic racing' because its layout favours the new power units. Hadjar made the comments during the summer break, having built a strong second Red Bull season with **regular top-six finishes**.
key_points: **Isack Hadjar** says F1's **2026 regulations** rank circuits by how much energy drivers can recover, not by how good the racing is.
Under the new rules, **Spa-Francorchamps** — one of F1's most iconic tracks — is now considered **'one of the worst' on the calendar** for that reason.
Hadjar praised the **Hungarian Grand Prix** as a return to 'classic racing' because its layout suits the new energy-recovery-focused cars.
The comments come from Red Bull's Hadjar, who has impressed with **consistent top-six finishes** in his second Red Bull season.
The remarks add to a growing driver debate about whether F1's 2026 technical rules are reshaping which tracks 'work' well, independent of their racing history.
cards.moot: Major rule changes in any competitive system don't just change who wins — they can quietly change which arenas (tracks, markets, formats) are even well-suited to the new rules, sometimes at odds with tradition.

depth.background: F1's **2026 regulations** introduced a major technical overhaul, including new power units that lean more heavily on **electrical energy recovery and deployment** — meaning how much energy a car can harvest and reuse now shapes lap time more than in previous eras. This changes which circuits produce good racing: tracks with long straights and heavy braking zones (which help energy recovery) tend to suit the new cars, while others don't. **Spa-Francorchamps** in Belgium is one of the sport's most historic and beloved circuits, making its slide down the 'best tracks' rankings under the new rules a sensitive topic among drivers and fans.
depth.why_it_matters: It's a rare on-record admission from a current driver that F1's biggest rules reset in years has an unintended side effect: reshuffling which historic circuits actually produce good racing, a concern that touches both the sport's technical direction and its relationship with its own history.
depth.ripple_effects: Expect more drivers and team principals to weigh in on the 2026 rules' effect on specific circuits, which could feed into F1's ongoing conversations with the FIA about mid-cycle rule tweaks or future calendar changes.
depth.why_now: The comments follow the Hungarian Grand Prix, which Hadjar used as a direct contrast to explain why some historic tracks now suit the cars less well.
depth.watch_next: Watch for FIA or F1 management response, and whether the debate resurfaces when the calendar returns to Spa in 2027.

key_terms.definition: F1's 2026 hybrid power units capture energy (e.g. from braking) and redeploy it for extra speed — tracks with more braking zones let cars use this system more, changing which circuits reward the new cars.

cards.title: Ben Duckett becomes The Hundred's leading run-scorer as Trent Rockets edge SunRisers Leeds
cards.what_happened: Batting first, Trent Rockets got a rapid start from **Aneurin Donald**, playing his first match of the campaign, who smashed **40 not out** off just 19 balls including three sixes. **Ben Duckett** then took over, reaching his third half-century of the tournament from 35 balls and adding a 50-run stand with Tim David before falling for **64** — a knock that made him the competition's leading run-scorer, overtaking England team-mate Phil Salt. Rockets posted **146 for 4**. In reply, Mitchell Marsh and Zak Crawley gave SunRisers Leeds a solid start, reaching 32 for 1 after the powerplay. Harry Brook threatened to take the game away before being caught by Duckett off Mohammad Amir for 46. Amir then struck twice more in the death overs, finishing with **2 for 20**, as SunRisers fell 5 runs short on **141 for 4**.
key_points: **Trent Rockets** beat **SunRisers Leeds** by **5 runs** at Trent Bridge to stay top of the Men's Hundred table.
**Ben Duckett** smashed **64** off 47 balls, overtaking Phil Salt to become the competition's **leading run-scorer**.

depth.ripple_effects: Trent Rockets strengthen their claim to a top finish and a home knockout match, while SunRisers Leeds slip further off the pace despite Marsh and Brook's form. Duckett's red-hot Hundred form adds to the selection conversation around England's white-ball top order.

depth.watch_next: Watch whether Trent Rockets can maintain their unbeaten run and hold off SunRisers Leeds and other challengers as the race for the knockout stages tightens.

cards.title: England's Danni Wyatt-Hodge ruled out of the rest of The Hundred with a calf tear
cards.what_happened: Wyatt-Hodge picked up the injury while playing through discomfort during MI London's narrow loss to Southern Brave, where she still top-scored with an unbeaten **52**. Scans have since confirmed a **left calf tear**, ruling her out for the rest of the tournament. The Hundred has confirmed **Ella Claridge**, a 23-year-old batter who plays for the USA internationally and for The Blaze domestically, as her replacement in the MI London squad. The news follows fellow captain **Sophie Devine's** calf injury elsewhere in the competition, meaning two teams have lost key top-order batters to the same type of injury within days of each other. Wyatt-Hodge's 93 runs this season, at an average of 46.50, had made her one of the few bright spots in an otherwise winless campaign for MI London.

cards.title: Rashid Khan claims his maiden Hundred five-wicket haul as MI London thump Manchester Super Giants Men
cards.what_happened: MI London posted 183 for 6, built around fifties from **Will Jacks (62)** and **Nicholas Pooran (54)**, at their home ground. In reply, Manchester Super Giants Men were bowled out for 138, with Rashid Khan tearing through their middle and lower order to finish with figures of 5 for 17 — his best-ever return in the tournament. **Aiden Markham's 50** was the only substantial score MSG could muster as they slipped to a 45-run defeat. The win moves MI London up to second place in the men's points table as the group stage heads toward its business end.

cards.title: India shakes up its coaching staff for the Sri Lanka Tests, naming a new fielding coach and losing an assistant to the IPL
cards.what_happened: The BCCI announced on Monday that **Subhadeep Ghosh**, a 57-year-old former Assam and Railways cricketer from Digboi, has been appointed India men's new fielding coach, replacing **T Dilip**, ahead of the upcoming two-Test tour of Sri Lanka. As a player, he represented Assam and Railways in 17 first-class and 17 List A matches. Separately, assistant coach **Ryan ten Doeschate** has left the India setup to join the **Kolkata Knight Riders** as Head of Cricket Strategy, an IPL role.

Ghosh, 57, from **Assam**, replaces **T Dilip** in the role.

depth.background: India's tour of Sri Lanka is an important early assignment for **Shubman Gill's** side in the current World Test Championship cycle, and it comes as the team is already dealing with a personnel setback — pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah was ruled out of the series with a knee injury. cards.title: Rain and Mohammad Abbas's shock axing shape Day 1 as West Indies close on 165/3 in the series-deciding 2nd Test
cards.what_happened: Rain repeatedly disrupted play on Day 1 of the series-deciding second Test between **West Indies and Pakistan** at the Queen's Park Oval — only **9.5 overs** were bowled before an early lunch forced by rain, with West Indies **49/1** at that point. West Indies, who won the series opener by 90 runs, need only a draw or win here to take the series; Pakistan must win to level it.
